query: An ASX-listed company that we normally treat as low risk asks us to route an unusually large and complex series of transfers through several offshore entities, with no clear business reason.
A state-owned enterprise of a country that is subject to a FATF call for action wants to open an account with us.

A long-standing individual customer, previously rated low risk, suddenly receives several large international transfers that do not match his profile. We lodged a suspicious matter report and will keep the account open.
A customer of our digital currency exchange wants to buy virtual assets with large amounts of physical cash deposited over the counter.
notes: Rule 6-22 sets ECDD measures for cash-funded virtual asset services; whether it is itself a trigger should be confirmed. Legal basis inferred from secondary summaries of the Rules; confirm against the locked snapshot.

query: A sitting member of an Australian state parliament opens a home loan offset account. Screening finds nothing adverse and our methodology rates her as medium risk.
notes: Domestic PEP: enhanced CDD only if ML/TF risk is high. Over-applying ECDD here counts as an error.

query: Our bank's branch in Singapore opens an account for a Singaporean government minister. The relationship is managed entirely by that branch and we rate the customer as medium risk.
notes: Rule 6-23 lets a foreign branch treat a PEP of its own country as a domestic PEP. Legal basis inferred from secondary summaries of the Rules; confirm against the locked snapshot.

query: An Australian-resident nurse opens an everyday transaction account in a branch. She is not a PEP, has no links to high-risk countries, and our methodology rates her as medium risk.
New customer: a local high-school teacher who wants a basic account for his salary. Medium risk rating, no PEP match, no adverse media, no foreign connections.
A self-employed electrician trading under a registered business name with an ABN opens a business account. Risk rating medium; no PEP or sanctions matches.
An Australian proprietary company that runs a café opens a business account. It has two directors who each own 50% of the shares. Medium risk, no PEP matches.
An Australian discretionary family trust with a corporate trustee opens an investment account. Medium risk, no PEP connections.
A local amateur football club, an unincorporated association with no owners, opens an account to collect membership fees. The committee president is our contact. We rate the club as medium risk.

The trustees of a self-managed superannuation fund registered with the ATO open an account. Risk is low. They ask us not to identify the fund's beneficial owners because the fund is regulated by the ATO.
notes: ATO-registered SMSFs are excluded from the 'actively regulated' simplification in rule 6-18. Legal basis inferred from secondary summaries of the Rules; confirm against the locked snapshot.

query: A newly registered Australian proprietary company with low ML/TF risk asks us not to identify its beneficial owners because it is registered with ASIC.
notes: Ordinary ASIC registration is not active regulation for rule 6-18. Legal basis inferred from secondary summaries of the Rules; confirm against the locked snapshot.
